A paper counts as a MATCH only if its title or abstract shows that it explicitly studies a relationship, effect, association, mechanism or method linking concept A and concept B: for example, it estimates the effect of one on the other, models how they interact, or applies a method named by one to the problem named by the other. A paper does NOT count if it merely mentions both concepts, lists them among many topics, or uses one only as background. Synonyms and close variants of a concept count as the concept.

- "match": true or false

- "relation": for a match, one of "supports", "challenges", "tests_mixed", "unclear" describing what the paper finds about the A–B link

Abstract This paper provides evidence of seasonal variation in individual Canadian provincial government bond returns. For the period of 1983–2003, holding period returns appear to fall significantly in the month of March. A trading strategy that took advantage of this seasonality would have out-performed a buy-and-hold strategy. The seasonal variation in Canadian bond returns correlates with seasonal movements in US 10-year Treasury bond yields, but not with factors originating in Canada. The results reveal significant seasonality in a major bond market that has not been analyzed previously, provide evidence of seasonality in one market spilling over into another market, and illustrate the importance of incorporating international factors in analyses of seasonality.
